title: 'Advanced Surgical Technologies Should Not Be Limited to Metro Cities': How These Founders Built a Homegrown Surgical GPS
excerpt: The GPS on your phone helps you find your way to a favourite restaurant, avoid traffic jams and take an unfamiliar road with confidence. It tells you where you are and helps you figure out where to go next. Now, imagine a similar guiding system inside an operating theatre, helping a surgeon navigate the delicate structures of the human brain or spine. That is the idea behind easyNav™, an image-guided surgical navigation system developed by Bengaluru-based health-tech company HRS Navigation. Using medical images to map a patient’s anatomy and track surgical instruments in real time, the technology helps surgeons understand where they are operating, particularly when working around sensitive nerves, blood vessels, and other critical structures. Founded in 2015 by Arpit Paliwal and Shweta Paliwal, HRS Navigation has developed an indigenous alternative to imported surgical navigation platforms. Its systems are now installed in more than 200 hospitals and have supported over 20,000 surgeries, according to the company. But the motivation behind the startup was not simply to build sophisticated medical technology. It was to address a question that Arpit encountered repeatedly: why should access to advanced surgical care depend so heavily on where a patient lives or how much they can afford? Why surgical precision needed to reach beyond metros An electronics engineer who also completed an executive programme at IIM Calcutta, Arpit spent around 11 years in an international role before deciding to build a medical technology company in India. His experience had given him an understanding of surgical navigation and the standards these systems needed to meet. It had also helped him recognise a gap in the market. Surgical navigation technology was already available internationally, but its adoption in India was constrained by more than the cost of purchasing a machine. Some imported systems required hospitals to buy recurring consumables for every procedure or upgrade their operating theatres to meet specific infrastructure requirements. For hospitals working with limited budgets, these expenses could make the technology difficult to sustain, particularly when treating patients who could not afford to pay much for surgery. Arpit recalls meeting families who were struggling to afford treatment. One interaction that stayed with him was that of a father who told him to proceed with his child’s operation, saying he would sell his house to arrange the money. “I have seen that kind of reality,” he says, describing the experiences that motivated him to build something for India. For him, the problem was not a lack of medical expertise. It was that the tools available to support complex procedures were not always accessible to the hospitals and patients who needed them. Simply reducing the price of an imported system would not necessarily solve this problem. The technology also had to work within the realities of Indian hospitals. “You need to adapt your system to work with the requirements of Indian infrastructure,” Arpit explains. That became a guiding principle for HRS Navigation. Starting with a small office and building its technology from the ground up, the founders set out to develop a system that could work with the equipment hospitals already had, without compromising on accuracy. It was a demanding undertaking in a field requiring extensive research, engineering, testing and regulatory compliance. Arpit says developing the technology from the prototype stage took years of work, including studying research papers and building the team’s technical expertise at a time when many of today’s AI tools were not available. The effort eventually led to easyNav™, designed around two priorities: precision that meets demanding clinical requirements and adaptability that makes the system practical for Indian hospitals. How does a GPS for surgeons work? To understand the technology, consider what happens when someone drives through an unfamiliar city without navigation. They must rely on signboards, landmarks and their own judgement to decide which road to take. A GPS adds another layer of information, showing their position in relation to the route and helping them correct their direction as they move. Surgical navigation applies a comparable principle inside the operating theatre, using medical imaging rather than road maps. Before surgery, CT scans provide detailed images of the patient’s anatomy. These images are used to create a reference for the procedure. During the operation, the navigation system tracks the position of surgical instruments and displays where they are in relation to that anatomy. This gives the surgeon an additional way to check the instrument’s position and trajectory, particularly when the target lies deep inside the body or close to structures that must be preserved. In brain surgery, for instance, the system can help a surgeon plan the route to a tumour and understand its relationship with important structures. In spine procedures, it can help determine the entry point and trajectory for placing screws. Dr Ranjit Deshmukh, consultant neurosurgeon at Sahyadri Hospital, Pune, explains that complex procedures have traditionally relied on anatomical landmarks, surgical experience and imaging during the operation to establish orientation. “Navigation provides an additional layer of anatomical guidance, helping the surgeon plan and execute these procedures with greater confidence,” he says. With easyNav™, Dr Deshmukh says he can understand where his instruments are in relation to the patient’s anatomy in real time. He particularly values this in complex brain surgeries involving deep-seated tumours, lesions near major blood vessels and procedures around the skull base. The technology can also support planning when a tumour lies close to functional areas of the brain. Information from techniques such as functional MRI and tractography can help surgeons understand these relationships and plan an approach that aims to remove as much of the tumour as safely possible while preserving critical functions. Importantly, navigation does not replace a surgeon’s judgement or experience. Instead, it provides additional information to support decisions during critical stages of an operation. Dr Deshmukh says he has used international navigation platforms for around 15 years and finds easyNav™ comparable in ease of use and overall workflow. "Once a surgical team becomes familiar with the system, it integrates into the procedure without adding unnecessary complexity," he adds. He has also noticed a reduction in uncertainty during many complex cases, although he cautions that complications and revision rates depend on several factors and cannot be attributed to a single technology. For Arpit, maintaining this precision while making the system affordable required extensive research into components, performance, and design. The team worked to meet international quality and regulatory parameters while developing a system suited to the infrastructure and needs of its intended users. From a small-town hospital to a mother’s second chance The value of this approach becomes clearer when the technology reaches hospitals beyond major metropolitan centres. Arpit recalls a surgeon in a small town in Maharashtra who used the system to operate on a young child from a farming family. The family had limited financial resources, and the surgeon operated for around Rs 10,000. When the surgeon shared the outcome with colleagues, they were surprised that such a procedure had been performed at a small centre. For Arpit, this was precisely the kind of change HRS Navigation had hoped to enable: helping skilled doctors access tools that can support complex surgery, even outside the largest hospitals. Another example comes from a trust hospital in Siddhagiri, Maharashtra, where the system has been in use for several years. According to Arpit, patients travel there from Maharashtra and neighbouring Karnataka because the hospital offers treatment at affordable rates. He recalls the case of a mother of three who had a brain tumour in a particularly difficult location. After approaching several larger hospitals, she eventually underwent surgery at the trust hospital. The procedure was successful, and she survived with her neurological functions preserved, Arpit says. Stories such as these illustrate why surgical navigation can matter beyond the operating theatre. When a hospital can offer complex procedures at an affordable cost, patients may have another option closer to home instead of having to travel to a major city. The impact is not limited to patients, either. Surgeons can gain confidence from being able to verify their instruments’ positions during difficult procedures. Arpit recalls how some senior surgeons initially questioned the system when its guidance differed from their expectations. After repeatedly checking its accuracy during operations, he says many began relying on it as an important part of their workflow. The company also points to a memorable procedure in Guntur in which a patient undergoing brain surgery remained awake and watched the film Baahubali. Unlike most brain surgeries, which are performed under general anaesthesia, an awake craniotomy requires the patient to remain conscious so doctors can monitor essential brain functions in real time. In this case, the patient was comfortable enough to watch a film while the surgical team monitored his responses using HRS Navigation's technology. "The case attracted widespread media attention," Arpit says. For the team, the procedure was a memorable demonstration of how image-guided technology can support surgeons in carefully selected operations where monitoring a patient's core functions is essential. HRS Navigation’s systems are now used across a wide range of hospitals, from smaller centres in places such as Guntur and Gorakhpur to larger institutions, including Apollo hospitals and AIIMS facilities. Dr Deshmukh believes such technologies can help narrow the gap between metro and non-metro healthcare facilities, provided hospitals also have the clinical expertise, training and technical support needed to use them effectively. “Advanced surgical technologies should not be limited to a few tertiary centres in major cities,” he says. Building medical technology in India, for the world Making precision technology accessible also means rethinking the business model behind it. Arpit says HRS Navigation has avoided recurring consumable costs for every procedure, a model he believes can help hospitals use the system without having to weigh the expense of additional supplies against a patient’s ability to pay. The company has also designed easyNav™ to work with existing operating theatre infrastructure, reducing the need for hospitals to make extensive changes before adopting the technology. These decisions are part of a larger ambition: to demonstrate that sophisticated medical devices can be designed and built in India without compromising on performance. Arpit says HRS Navigation has received international recognition for its product design, including an iF Design Award from Germany and an A’ Design Award from Italy. The company has also been selected by India’s Department of Science and Technology for recognition linked to the country’s 75 years of independence. For him, these milestones matter because medical technology made in India should be judged on what it can achieve, rather than assumptions about where it comes from. “We have taken a long path of doing it from India,” he says, describing the company’s ambition to become globally respected. That ambition is closely tied to the reason he started the company in the first place. The goal is not only to compete with established international manufacturers but also to make precision healthcare more accessible to people who might otherwise struggle to reach it. Surgical navigation cannot, on its own, solve every challenge in healthcare. The right equipment must work alongside skilled surgeons, trained teams, reliable support and hospitals that patients can afford to access. "But when those pieces come together, technology can expand what a hospital is equipped to offer and give surgeons another tool to make informed decisions," adds Arpit. For the family trying to afford an operation, the surgeon working in a smaller town, or the patient who needs a complex procedure without travelling hundreds of kilometres, that difference can be deeply personal. And that is the promise behind HRS Navigation’s homegrown GPS for surgeons: not simply helping doctors find their way through the human body, but helping more patients find their way to advanced surgical care. title: Telangana launches startup challenge, invites solutions to 18 key public sector problems
excerpt: HYDERABAD: The Government of Telangana has launched the Telangana Innovation Startup Challenge (TISC) at the Invest Telangana curtain-raiser in New Delhi, inviting startups and entrepreneurs to develop practical, cost-effective solutions for real-world challenges in critical sectors. The initiative aims to move beyond ideas to implementation, enabling promising solutions to be piloted, deployed and adopted by […]HYDERABAD: The Government of Telangana has launched the Telangana Innovation Startup Challenge (TISC) at the Invest Telangana curtain-raiser in New Delhi, inviting startups and entrepreneurs to develop practical, cost-effective solutions for real-world challenges in critical sectors. The initiative aims to move beyond ideas to implementation, enabling promising solutions to be piloted, deployed and adopted by the government. Successful participants will get opportunities for government contracts and a global showcase at the Invest Telangana Global Summit 2026. The government has identified 18 specific challenges across energy, agriculture, healthcare, education and urban infrastructure. Anudeep Durishetty, Joint Secretary, ITE&C Department, said, "We are looking for practical, cost-effective solutions that make a meaningful difference to people's lives. Win the Telangana Innovation Startup Challenge TISC and you get a Government contract to take your solution to the real world." Key challenges The identified problems include developing a solar-powered irrigation pump or retrofit kit for deep borewells that is 30% cheaper, with theft-resistant panels, to reduce the ₹14,000 crore annual free-power burden, rapid food-adulteration test kits and AI-enabled kitchen hygiene monitoring for residential hostels, and satellite-based monitoring systems to detect new encroachments on lakes and government land. Other urban and agricultural challenges include vehicle-mounted cameras for automated pothole mapping and a durable repair mix, a handheld needle-free haemoglobin meter for mass anaemia screening, an AI-enabled Telugu reading assessment for government schools, and satellite- and app-based crop mapping at the survey-number level. For the power sector, the challenges include AI tools to map feeder networks and rank infrastructure upgrades, drone-based monitoring of grid assets with AI detecting cracks and hotspots, AI assessment of solar potential at substations, AI validation of material quality against purchase-order specifications, revenue assurance analytics to detect power theft, personalised billing assistance in Telugu, and an auto connection cost estimator. Other power-sector challenges focus on AI risk-scoring for project execution, forecasting solar generation for rooftop management, storm outage prediction and crew dispatch, and predictive maintenance of assets. Timeline Startups must submit their solutions by November 20, 2026. Evaluation and shortlisting will be based on feasibility, innovation, affordability, scalability and public impact. Shortlisted teams will pitch to the departments at Demo Day on December 1, 2026, at the T-Hub campus in Hyderabad. Selected startups will showcase their solutions from December 7 to 9, 2026, as a curtain raiser to the Invest Telangana Global Summit 2026, with opportunities to pilot and secure potential government procurement. ]]>

title: Centre urges states to step up coal gasification, mining of critical minerals
excerpt: New Delhi, November 5 (IANS): Union Coal and Mines Minister G. Kishan Reddy on Thursday highlighted the need to accelerate coal gasification for the optimum utilisation of India's abundant coal resources and flagged the strategic importance of critical minerals in the evolving global geopolitical landscape. Addressing the conference of Mining Ministers on reforms in the mines and coal sector, being held in Goa, the minister said coal gasification would unlock the economic value of domestic coal, promote industrial diversification, generate employment, and strengthen the country's long-term energy security. He urged coal-bearing states to actively facilitate investments, support infrastructure development, and accelerate project implementation to realise the sector's immense potential. Highlighting the strategic importance of critical minerals, the minister stressed the need to strengthen domestic exploration, mining, processing, refining, and recycling capabilities. He emphasised that developing a self-reliant mineral ecosystem is essential to reducing import dependence and strengthening India's strategic and economic resilience. Emphasising the transformative role of technology, Reddy called upon state governments to harness Artificial Intelligence (AI), digitalisation and advanced technological solutions across exploration, mine operations and mineral recovery. He highlighted that technology-driven practices would improve productivity, operational efficiency and sustainability in the mining and coal sectors. The minister urged states to expedite the operationalisation of auctioned mines, accelerate the auction of new blocks, expand exploration activities and adopt technology-driven practices to unlock the full potential of their mineral resources. He also highlighted how mining sector reforms have strengthened state economies, attracted investments, generated employment opportunities and enhanced revenue generation, while promoting development in mining-affected regions. Reddy called for stronger coordination between the Centre and states to unlock India's mineral and coal potential, strengthen the mining ecosystem and ensure sustainable and inclusive growth. He expressed confidence that collective efforts and a shared roadmap would take India's mining and coal sectors to new heights. Addressing the conference, Coal Secretary Vikram Dev Dutt highlighted the significant progress made by India's coal sector and its vital role in strengthening the country's energy security and driving economic growth. He noted that domestic coal production had surpassed one billion tonnes for the second consecutive year, marking a significant achievement in India's journey towards energy self-reliance and reducing dependence on imported coal. He highlighted coal gasification as a major opportunity for value addition, industrial diversification and employment generation. Stressing the importance of technology, digitalisation, sustainable mining practices and efficient logistics, the Secretary called for stronger Centre-State collaboration to unlock the full potential of India's coal and mineral resources. The Union Ministry of Mines is organising the 4th Conference of Mining Ministers on November 5 and 6 in Goa, bringing together Mining Ministers from various states and senior officials from the Central and state governments. The conference provided an important platform for interaction and exchange of views on various aspects of the mining sector.

title: Play Forward 2026: India and Germany script a new sporting partnership for the future
excerpt: In its pursuit of the ‘Viksit Bharat’ milestone in 2047, the country has steadfastly followed the ‘Atmanirbhar Bharat’ template. From Covid 19, higher US tariffs, to the oil crisis, Bharat has converted every crisis into an opportunity. The dawn of 2026 saw India signing the Indo-European Free Trade Agreement, which many domain experts in the world treat as the mother of all the deals. “When Dronacharya placed a wooden bird on a tree and asked his students what they saw, while others saw the tree, sky and branches, Arjun stated he saw only the bird’s before striking it. While most of the world is in the deep turmoil, India like a monk on deep meditation has its focus and efforts totally fixated on Bhartiyta and Viksit Bharat by 2047’- remarked one of the members of the Indian diaspora who had come to attend the Bosch Play Forward- the Indo-German Sports and Business Conclave in the DFB Campus in Frankfurt Germany on October 30, 2026. If the Indo-European Free Trade Agreement has to realise its true potential, the relationship between India and Germany has to be the engine to the growth story. In the recent months, India and Germany strategic relationship has reached historic milestones and there has been noticeable expansion of the Indo-German Strategic Partnership. As we say in the terminology of the sports, the field is wide open and the atmosphere is conducive for both the teams to make the most out of it. Quoting extensively from the ancient Indian texts, Ketkar emphasized on how vedic ecosystem at one point of time enlightened the whole world and thereby we need to look inward to achieve our target of being a developed sporting country. He talked about the lost literature in the medieval age when the country and Indian civilization was invaded by the foreigners. Incidentally, this was the time when the great German minds in sports like Johann Christoph Friedrich GutsMuths- the father of gymnastics made a seminal contribution in terms of literature and thereby laid a solid sporting foundation for the future generation. The beauty of the ‘Play Forward Initiative’ and the conclave lied in the preaching juxtaposed with the on ground practical reality. The participants were walking the talk. In one of the engrossing sessions, renowned German Sports Scientist and Innovator, Jan Mayer and former chairman of the National Statistical Commission and Padma Shri Bimal Kumar Roy in their unique jugalbandi highlighted the importance of the evidence led approaches and structured pathways for developing sporting talents. The proof of the pudding is in the eating. Jan Mayer has been part of the Olympics Sub-committee of Germany which prepared the German athletes for the future Olympics. In India, in collaboration with the famous German company Bosch, Ian Mayer and Kaushik Maulik has successfully executed psycho analytics-based technology in identifying talents as the trial run. The conclave also featured Mularajsinh Chudasama, General Secretary of the Gujarat Football Association, who also talked about the technology and its role in identifying talents in a huge and diverse country like India and thereby staging the stage for unearthing the future sporting stars. If India aspires to be a strong and serious sporting power by 2047, all wheels need to be aligned together and sports broadcasting is the crucial cog in this wheel. title: Gujarat to set up Export Promotion Council to help MSMEs, startups access global markets
excerpt: Gandhinagar, Nov 5 (IANS) The Gujarat government has approved the establishment of a dedicated Gujarat Export Promotion Council (GEPC) to help industries, particularly micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) and startups, access international markets and increase the state's exports. The council will function as a special purpose vehicle (SPV) under the Industries and Mines Department and provide a single institutional platform for export-related guidance, market access, technical assistance, finance and logistics support. It will also prepare district-specific export promotion plans to identify local products and industries with the potential to reach international markets. According to a government resolution dated November 3, the GEPC will be established as a wholly state-owned, non-profit private limited company under Section 8 of the Companies Act, 2013, with its registered office in Gandhinagar. Custom Ad: Multiplex The proposal follows recommendations by a task force constituted to enhance the competitiveness of Gujarat's manufacturing sector, which identified export development as one of the three key pillars of industrial growth. The Gujarat State Institution for Transformation (GRIT) prepared a report in May 2025 recommending the establishment of a dedicated export promotion institution. The proposal was subsequently approved by the state government following its submission by the Industries Commissionerate. The council will focus on helping smaller enterprises overcome difficulties in accessing foreign markets, including limited awareness of international market requirements, export procedures, regulations and mandatory certifications. It will provide assistance in identifying overseas markets, developing entry strategies, business consultancy, mentoring and handholding. It will also organise training programmes, workshops, seminars and skill development initiatives for entrepreneurs and exporters. Through partnerships with government institutions and trade organisations, the council will facilitate participation in domestic and international trade fairs and marketing programmes. To ease export-related processes, the GEPC plans to develop digital trade platforms, an exporter portal, common facility centres, incubation centres, testing and certification facilities and logistics support systems. Exporters will also receive assistance with product quality testing, international certifications, trade finance, insurance, pre-shipment and post-shipment financial facilities and supply chain management. The council will provide guidance on market intelligence, trade analytics, product development, branding and compliance with international regulations. A major component of its work will be preparing a separate District Export Promotion Plan for every district, in line with the state's Export Promotion Strategy. These plans will be periodically updated after assessing district-level production capacities, industrial specialisations, market demand and export potential. District Export Promotion Councils (DEPCs), along with regional and sector-specific institutions, will coordinate and monitor export-related activities. The government also plans to undertake international branding and marketing campaigns to establish Gujarat-manufactured products as recognised global brands. Alongside promoting exports, the council will work to reduce import dependence by identifying sectors relying on imports and extending technical, financial and advisory support to manufacturers to develop domestic alternatives. The GEPC will also encourage the use of emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence (AI), blockchain, digitisation and Industry 4.0, in export-related processes. It will promote sustainable exports through green technologies, environmentally friendly products and compliance with international environmental standards. Support will also be extended to exporters seeking intellectual property rights, including patents, trademarks and copyrights, in foreign markets. The council will assist in addressing international trade disputes, legal issues and non-tariff barriers. The company's initial authorised and paid-up capital has been fixed at Rs one lakh, with the entire share capital to be held in the name of the Governor through authorised nominees of the state government. It will be empowered to raise funds and secure loans from banks and financial institutions in accordance with legal provisions. The board will have between three and 15 members, with the Chief Secretary serving as its chairperson and the Additional Chief Secretary, Principal Secretary or Secretary of the Industries and Mines Department as vice-chairperson. The Industries Commissioner will serve as managing director. Representatives from the Ports and Transport Department, Cottage and Rural Industries Department, Agriculture, Farmers Welfare and Cooperation Department, MSME Commissionerate, Gujarat Industrial Development Corporation (GIDC), iNDEXTb, Gujarat Infrastructure Development Board and Finance Department will also be part of the board. The council is intended to bring export promotion activities under a common institutional framework and connect production capabilities across Gujarat's districts with international markets. --IANS mys/dpb

title: 'Advanced Surgical Technologies Should Not Be Limited to Metro Cities': How These Founders Built a Homegrown Surgical GPS
excerpt: The GPS on your phone helps you find your way to a favourite restaurant, avoid traffic jams and take an unfamiliar road with confidence. It tells you where you are and helps you figure out where to go next. Now, imagine a similar guiding system inside an operating theatre, helping a surgeon navigate the delicate structures of the human brain or spine. That is the idea behind easyNav™, an image-guided surgical navigation system developed by Bengaluru-based health-tech company HRS Navigation. Using medical images to map a patient’s anatomy and track surgical instruments in real time, the technology helps surgeons understand where they are operating, particularly when working around sensitive nerves, blood vessels, and other critical structures. Founded in 2015 by Arpit Paliwal and Shweta Paliwal, HRS Navigation has developed an indigenous alternative to imported surgical navigation platforms. Its systems are now installed in more than 200 hospitals and have supported over 20,000 surgeries, according to the company. But the motivation behind the startup was not simply to build sophisticated medical technology. It was to address a question that Arpit encountered repeatedly: why should access to advanced surgical care depend so heavily on where a patient lives or how much they can afford? Why surgical precision needed to reach beyond metros An electronics engineer who also completed an executive programme at IIM Calcutta, Arpit spent around 11 years in an international role before deciding to build a medical technology company in India. His experience had given him an understanding of surgical navigation and the standards these systems needed to meet. It had also helped him recognise a gap in the market. Surgical navigation technology was already available internationally, but its adoption in India was constrained by more than the cost of purchasing a machine. Some imported systems required hospitals to buy recurring consumables for every procedure or upgrade their operating theatres to meet specific infrastructure requirements. For hospitals working with limited budgets, these expenses could make the technology difficult to sustain, particularly when treating patients who could not afford to pay much for surgery. Arpit recalls meeting families who were struggling to afford treatment. One interaction that stayed with him was that of a father who told him to proceed with his child’s operation, saying he would sell his house to arrange the money. “I have seen that kind of reality,” he says, describing the experiences that motivated him to build something for India. For him, the problem was not a lack of medical expertise. It was that the tools available to support complex procedures were not always accessible to the hospitals and patients who needed them. Simply reducing the price of an imported system would not necessarily solve this problem. The technology also had to work within the realities of Indian hospitals. “You need to adapt your system to work with the requirements of Indian infrastructure,” Arpit explains. That became a guiding principle for HRS Navigation. Starting with a small office and building its technology from the ground up, the founders set out to develop a system that could work with the equipment hospitals already had, without compromising on accuracy. It was a demanding undertaking in a field requiring extensive research, engineering, testing and regulatory compliance. Arpit says developing the technology from the prototype stage took years of work, including studying research papers and building the team’s technical expertise at a time when many of today’s AI tools were not available. The effort eventually led to easyNav™, designed around two priorities: precision that meets demanding clinical requirements and adaptability that makes the system practical for Indian hospitals. How does a GPS for surgeons work? To understand the technology, consider what happens when someone drives through an unfamiliar city without navigation. They must rely on signboards, landmarks and their own judgement to decide which road to take. A GPS adds another layer of information, showing their position in relation to the route and helping them correct their direction as they move. Surgical navigation applies a comparable principle inside the operating theatre, using medical imaging rather than road maps. Before surgery, CT scans provide detailed images of the patient’s anatomy. These images are used to create a reference for the procedure. During the operation, the navigation system tracks the position of surgical instruments and displays where they are in relation to that anatomy. This gives the surgeon an additional way to check the instrument’s position and trajectory, particularly when the target lies deep inside the body or close to structures that must be preserved. In brain surgery, for instance, the system can help a surgeon plan the route to a tumour and understand its relationship with important structures. In spine procedures, it can help determine the entry point and trajectory for placing screws. Dr Ranjit Deshmukh, consultant neurosurgeon at Sahyadri Hospital, Pune, explains that complex procedures have traditionally relied on anatomical landmarks, surgical experience and imaging during the operation to establish orientation. “Navigation provides an additional layer of anatomical guidance, helping the surgeon plan and execute these procedures with greater confidence,” he says. With easyNav™, Dr Deshmukh says he can understand where his instruments are in relation to the patient’s anatomy in real time. He particularly values this in complex brain surgeries involving deep-seated tumours, lesions near major blood vessels and procedures around the skull base. The technology can also support planning when a tumour lies close to functional areas of the brain. Information from techniques such as functional MRI and tractography can help surgeons understand these relationships and plan an approach that aims to remove as much of the tumour as safely possible while preserving critical functions. Importantly, navigation does not replace a surgeon’s judgement or experience. Instead, it provides additional information to support decisions during critical stages of an operation. Dr Deshmukh says he has used international navigation platforms for around 15 years and finds easyNav™ comparable in ease of use and overall workflow. "Once a surgical team becomes familiar with the system, it integrates into the procedure without adding unnecessary complexity," he adds. He has also noticed a reduction in uncertainty during many complex cases, although he cautions that complications and revision rates depend on several factors and cannot be attributed to a single technology. For Arpit, maintaining this precision while making the system affordable required extensive research into components, performance, and design. The team worked to meet international quality and regulatory parameters while developing a system suited to the infrastructure and needs of its intended users. From a small-town hospital to a mother’s second chance The value of this approach becomes clearer when the technology reaches hospitals beyond major metropolitan centres. Arpit recalls a surgeon in a small town in Maharashtra who used the system to operate on a young child from a farming family. The family had limited financial resources, and the surgeon operated for around Rs 10,000. When the surgeon shared the outcome with colleagues, they were surprised that such a procedure had been performed at a small centre. For Arpit, this was precisely the kind of change HRS Navigation had hoped to enable: helping skilled doctors access tools that can support complex surgery, even outside the largest hospitals. Another example comes from a trust hospital in Siddhagiri, Maharashtra, where the system has been in use for several years. According to Arpit, patients travel there from Maharashtra and neighbouring Karnataka because the hospital offers treatment at affordable rates. He recalls the case of a mother of three who had a brain tumour in a particularly difficult location. After approaching several larger hospitals, she eventually underwent surgery at the trust hospital. The procedure was successful, and she survived with her neurological functions preserved, Arpit says. Stories such as these illustrate why surgical navigation can matter beyond the operating theatre. When a hospital can offer complex procedures at an affordable cost, patients may have another option closer to home instead of having to travel to a major city. The impact is not limited to patients, either. Surgeons can gain confidence from being able to verify their instruments’ positions during difficult procedures. Arpit recalls how some senior surgeons initially questioned the system when its guidance differed from their expectations. After repeatedly checking its accuracy during operations, he says many began relying on it as an important part of their workflow. The company also points to a memorable procedure in Guntur in which a patient undergoing brain surgery remained awake and watched the film Baahubali. Unlike most brain surgeries, which are performed under general anaesthesia, an awake craniotomy requires the patient to remain conscious so doctors can monitor essential brain functions in real time. In this case, the patient was comfortable enough to watch a film while the surgical team monitored his responses using HRS Navigation's technology. "The case attracted widespread media attention," Arpit says. For the team, the procedure was a memorable demonstration of how image-guided technology can support surgeons in carefully selected operations where monitoring a patient's core functions is essential. HRS Navigation’s systems are now used across a wide range of hospitals, from smaller centres in places such as Guntur and Gorakhpur to larger institutions, including Apollo hospitals and AIIMS facilities. Dr Deshmukh believes such technologies can help narrow the gap between metro and non-metro healthcare facilities, provided hospitals also have the clinical expertise, training and technical support needed to use them effectively. “Advanced surgical technologies should not be limited to a few tertiary centres in major cities,” he says. Building medical technology in India, for the world Making precision technology accessible also means rethinking the business model behind it. Arpit says HRS Navigation has avoided recurring consumable costs for every procedure, a model he believes can help hospitals use the system without having to weigh the expense of additional supplies against a patient’s ability to pay. The company has also designed easyNav™ to work with existing operating theatre infrastructure, reducing the need for hospitals to make extensive changes before adopting the technology. These decisions are part of a larger ambition: to demonstrate that sophisticated medical devices can be designed and built in India without compromising on performance. Arpit says HRS Navigation has received international recognition for its product design, including an iF Design Award from Germany and an A’ Design Award from Italy. The company has also been selected by India’s Department of Science and Technology for recognition linked to the country’s 75 years of independence. For him, these milestones matter because medical technology made in India should be judged on what it can achieve, rather than assumptions about where it comes from. “We have taken a long path of doing it from India,” he says, describing the company’s ambition to become globally respected. That ambition is closely tied to the reason he started the company in the first place. The goal is not only to compete with established international manufacturers but also to make precision healthcare more accessible to people who might otherwise struggle to reach it. Surgical navigation cannot, on its own, solve every challenge in healthcare. The right equipment must work alongside skilled surgeons, trained teams, reliable support and hospitals that patients can afford to access. "But when those pieces come together, technology can expand what a hospital is equipped to offer and give surgeons another tool to make informed decisions," adds Arpit. For the family trying to afford an operation, the surgeon working in a smaller town, or the patient who needs a complex procedure without travelling hundreds of kilometres, that difference can be deeply personal. And that is the promise behind HRS Navigation’s homegrown GPS for surgeons: not simply helping doctors find their way through the human body, but helping more patients find their way to advanced surgical care.
